p.src: As Cao Cao fled in panic, a force arrived from due south: Xiahou Dun had brought troops to his rescue and intercepted Lü Bu in fierce battle. They fought until dusk, when rain began pouring down, and each side withdrew and dispersed its troops. Cao Cao returned to camp, richly rewarded Dian Wei, and promoted him to Commandant of the Army.

p.src: Meanwhile, Lü Bu returned to camp and conferred with Chen Gong. Chen Gong said, “In Puyang there is a wealthy household, the Tian family, with servants numbering in the thousands; it is the foremost house in the commandery. Have him secretly send someone with a letter to Cao Cao’s camp, saying that Marquis Lü is cruel and inhumane, that the people bitterly resent him, and that he now intends to move his army to Liyang, leaving only Gao Shun in the city; Cao Cao may advance by night, and I shall answer from within. If Cao Cao comes, lure him into the city, set fire at all four gates, and station ambushes outside. Though Cao Cao has talent enough to order heaven and earth, how could he escape from such a place?” Lü Bu followed his plan and secretly instructed the Tian family to send a man directly to Cao Cao’s camp. Cao Cao, hesitant after his recent defeat, was suddenly told that a man from the Tian family had arrived. The man presented a secret letter saying, “Lü Bu has gone to Liyang, and the city lies undefended. I earnestly beg you to come swiftly; I shall answer from within. A white flag bearing the large character ‘Righteousness’ will be raised on the wall as our secret signal.” Cao Cao rejoiced. “Heaven has delivered Puyang into my hands!” he exclaimed. He richly rewarded the messenger and at once prepared his army to march. Liu Ye said, “Though Lü Bu lacks cunning, Chen Gong is full of schemes. I fear there may be deceit in this; we cannot fail to guard against it. If my lord wishes to go, divide the army into three columns: two are to lie in ambush outside the city as support, and only one should enter.”

p.src: Cao Cao accepted his advice, divided the army into three columns, and came beneath the walls of Puyang. Cao Cao first rode forward to observe the city. Banners stood everywhere upon its walls, and at the corner of the west gate was a white flag bearing the character “Righteousness.” He rejoiced inwardly. At midday the city gate opened, and two generals led troops out to fight: Hou Cheng commanded the van and Gao Shun the rear. Cao Cao immediately sent Dian Wei forth to charge straight at Hou Cheng. Unable to withstand him, Hou Cheng wheeled his horse and fled toward the city. Dian Wei pursued him to the drawbridge. Gao Shun could not stop him either, and both men retreated into the city. Amid their ranks, a soldier seized the moment to slip through the lines and approach Cao Cao, saying he was an envoy of the Tian family and presenting a secret letter. It said, “Tonight, during the first watch, a gong will sound upon the walls as the signal; then you may advance. I shall surrender the gate.” Cao Cao assigned Xiahou Dun to lead troops on the left and Cao Hong on the right; he himself would enter the city with four generals—Xiahou Yuan, Li Dian, Yue Jin, and Dian Wei—and their men. Li Dian said, “My lord, remain outside the city for now and allow us to enter first.” Cao Cao rebuked him: “If I do not go myself, who will be willing to advance?” He then took the lead and marched his troops straight into the city.

p.src: It was about the first watch, and the moon had not yet risen. Suddenly a conch horn sounded above the west gate, shouts erupted, torches flared chaotically on the walls, the city gate opened wide, and the drawbridge dropped. Cao Cao spurred his horse in ahead of all the others. He rode straight to the provincial offices without seeing a single person along the road. Realizing it was a trap, Cao Cao hurriedly wheeled his horse and shouted, “Retreat!” A cannon blast sounded from the provincial offices, and raging fires at all four gates roared skyward; gongs and drums thundered together, and the battle cries surged like rivers overturning and seas boiling. Zhang Liao emerged from an eastern alley and Zang Ba from a western one, attacking from both sides and falling upon Cao Cao’s troops. Cao Cao fled toward the north gate, but Hao Meng and Cao Xing sprang out beside the road and attacked him again. Cao Cao hastened toward the south gate, where Gao Shun and Hou Cheng blocked his way. Dian Wei glared and clenched his teeth, then fought his way out. Gao Shun and Hou Cheng turned and fled out of the city.

p.src: Dian Wei fought his way to the drawbridge, but when he looked back Cao Cao was nowhere to be seen. He turned and fought back into the city, meeting Li Dian beneath the gate. Dian Wei asked, “Where is our lord?” Li Dian replied, “I cannot find him either.” Dian Wei said, “Stay outside the city and urge the relief troops forward. I shall go in and find our lord.” Li Dian departed. Dian Wei fought back into the city and searched, but could not find Cao Cao; he fought his way out once more, and beside the moat he encountered Yue Jin. Yue Jin asked, “Where is our lord?” Dian Wei replied, “I have gone in and out twice, but cannot find him.” Yue Jin said, “Let us fight our way in together and rescue our lord!” When the two reached the gate, flaming missiles rolled down from the wall. Yue Jin’s horse could not enter, but Dian Wei braved the smoke and burst through the flames, fought his way inside again, and searched everywhere.

p.src: Meanwhile, after Cao Cao saw Dian Wei fight his way out, enemy troops and horsemen closed in from every side, preventing him from escaping by the south gate; he turned again toward the north gate, where in the firelight he came face to face with Lü Bu, charging on horseback with halberd leveled. Cao Cao covered his face with one hand, lashed his horse, and galloped straight past. Lü Bu spurred after him, struck Cao Cao’s helmet with his halberd, and demanded, “Where is Cao Cao?” Cao Cao pointed ahead and replied, “He is the man riding the yellow horse.”

p.src: Hearing this, Lü Bu abandoned Cao Cao and galloped ahead in pursuit. Cao Cao wheeled his horse and fled toward the east gate, where he met Dian Wei. Dian Wei guarded Cao Cao and carved a bloody path to the city gate. The flames there raged fiercely; bundles of firewood had been pushed down from the wall, and fire covered the ground. Dian Wei swept the burning debris aside with his halberds and galloped first through smoke and flame. Cao Cao followed him out. Just as he reached the gateway, a burning beam collapsed from above and struck his warhorse across the hindquarters, bringing it crashing to the ground. Cao Cao caught the beam in his hands and thrust it to the ground, but his arms, beard, and hair were all burned.

p.src: Dian Wei turned his horse back to rescue him, and at that very moment Xiahou Yuan also arrived. Together they lifted Cao Cao to safety and broke through the flames. Cao Cao mounted Xiahou Yuan’s horse, while Dian Wei cut open a broad path for their escape. The confused battle continued until daybreak, and only then did Cao Cao return to camp. All the generals prostrated themselves and asked after his health. Cao Cao threw back his head and laughed. “I mistakenly fell for a common fellow’s trick, but I shall certainly repay him!” Guo Jia said, “Then the plan must be put into action swiftly.” Cao Cao said, “I shall now turn his own stratagem against him. Spread the false report that I was burned, that the fire’s poison overwhelmed me, and that I died at the fifth watch. Lü Bu will surely lead his troops here to attack. I shall conceal troops in the hills of Maling and strike when half his army has crossed; then Lü Bu can be captured.” Guo Jia said, “An excellent plan indeed!” The soldiers were therefore ordered to don mourning dress and hold funeral rites, falsely proclaiming Cao Cao’s death. Soon someone went to Puyang and reported to Lü Bu that Cao Cao’s body had been burned and injured, and that he had died upon reaching camp. Lü Bu immediately mustered his army and charged toward Maling Hill. As he neared Cao Cao’s camp, a drum sounded and ambushing troops rose on every side. Lü Bu fought desperately and escaped, but lost a great many men and horses; he retreated in defeat to Puyang, where he held fast and would not come out.

p.src: That year, swarms of locusts suddenly arose and devoured all the grain crops. Throughout the lands east of the passes, a single hu of grain cost fifty strings of cash, and the people ate one another. With his army’s provisions exhausted, Cao Cao withdrew to Juancheng to remain there for the time being. Lü Bu likewise led his troops out to camp at Shanyang in search of provisions. Thus the two sides suspended hostilities for the time being.

p.src: Meanwhile, Tao Qian was in Xuzhou. Now sixty-three years old, he suddenly fell ill, and as his condition steadily worsened, he summoned Mi Zhu and Chen Deng to discuss affairs. Mi Zhu said, “Cao Cao’s army withdrew only because Lü Bu attacked Yan Province. Now hostilities have ceased because of the famine, but Cao Cao will surely return next spring. Twice, my lord, you wished to yield your office to Liu Xuande. At the time you were still in good health, and so Xuande refused to accept it; now that your illness has become grave, you should bestow it upon him here and now, face to face; Xuande will surely not refuse.”

p.src: Tao Qian was overjoyed and sent a man to Xiaopei to invite Liu Xuande to discuss military affairs. Xuande brought Guan Yu and Zhang Fei with several dozen horsemen to Xuzhou, where Tao Qian had him shown into his private chamber. After Xuande had inquired after his health, Tao Qian said, “I have invited you here for no other reason than that my illness is now critical, and I may not last another day. I earnestly beg you to put the cities of the Han realm first and accept the seal and insignia of Xuzhou. Then I may close my eyes in peace!” Xuande said, “You have two sons. Why not pass it on to them?” Tao Qian replied, “My elder son is Shang and my younger son Ying, but neither possesses the ability for such a charge. After my death, I still hope you will instruct them; on no account let them take charge of the province.” Xuande said, “How could I possibly bear so great a responsibility?” Tao Qian said, “I shall recommend one man who can assist you. He is from Beihai; his surname is Sun, his given name Qian, and his courtesy name Gongyou. You may appoint him as an aide.” Then he said to Mi Zhu, “Lord Liu is a hero of this age. You must serve him well.”

p.src: Still Xuande declined, and Tao Qian pointed to his heart and died. When the whole army had finished mourning, they presented the seal and insignia to Xuande. Xuande firmly refused them. The next day, the people of Xuzhou thronged before the government offices, weeping and bowing as they cried, “If Governor Liu will not take charge of this commandery, none of us will be able to live in peace!” Guan Yu and Zhang Fei also urged him again and again. Xuande then agreed to assume temporary charge of Xuzhou. He took Sun Qian and Mi Zhu as his assistants and appointed Chen Deng to his staff. He brought all the troops and horses from Xiaopei into the city and posted proclamations to reassure the people. At the same time, he made arrangements for the funeral. Xuande and every officer and soldier donned mourning and held a grand memorial sacrifice. After the rites, Tao Qian was buried on the plain by the Yellow River. Tao Qian’s final memorial was then submitted to the imperial court.

p.src: In Juancheng, Cao Cao learned that Tao Qian had died and Liu Xuande had assumed the governorship of Xuzhou. Enraged, he cried, “My vengeance is still unfulfilled, yet without expending the effort of half an arrow you have gained Xuzhou at your ease! I shall first kill Liu Bei, then mutilate Tao Qian’s corpse, and so avenge my late father!” He immediately issued orders to raise an army on an appointed day and march against Xuzhou. Xun Yu came forward to remonstrate: “In former times, Emperor Gaozu secured Guanzhong and Emperor Guangwu held Henei; both planted deep roots and made firm their foundations, and thereby brought order to the realm. They could advance and defeat their enemies or withdraw and defend securely; thus, though they met with hardship, they ultimately accomplished their great enterprises. My lord first established his cause in Yanzhou, and the lands of the Yellow River and the Ji are strategic centers of the realm. They are the Guanzhong and Henei of former times. If you now go to seize Xuzhou, leaving many troops behind will leave too few for the campaign, while leaving only a few will allow Lü Bu to invade the undefended province. Then Yanzhou will be lost. And if you fail to gain Xuzhou, where will you have left to return to? Though Tao Qian is now dead, Liu Bei already holds the province. The people of Xuzhou have submitted to Liu Bei and will surely aid him in a fight to the death. For you to abandon Yanzhou and seek Xuzhou would be to forsake the great for the small, leave the root in pursuit of the branches, and exchange security for danger. I beg you to consider it carefully.” Cao Cao said, “This year’s harvest has failed and provisions are scarce. It is no sound policy for the soldiers to remain here idle.” Xun Yu replied, “It would be better to campaign eastward in the territory of Chen and let the army feed itself there. In Runan and Yingchuan, remnants of the Yellow Turbans such as He Yi and Huang Shao have plundered the commanderies and amassed much gold, silk, and grain. These bandits will also be easy to defeat. Defeat them and seize their grain to provision the whole army; the court will rejoice and the people will be pleased. That is a course in accord with Heaven.”

p.src: Cao Cao was pleased and accepted his counsel. He left Xiahou Dun and Cao Ren to guard Juancheng and the surrounding places, while he personally led the army to seize the territory of Chen and then advance into Runan and Yingchuan. When the Yellow Turban leaders He Yi and Huang Shao learned that Cao Cao’s army was approaching, they led their followers out to meet it, and the two forces encountered each other at Mount Yang. Though the bandit army was numerous, it was merely a rabble of scoundrels, with neither units nor battle formations. Cao Cao ordered his powerful bows and crossbows to hold them at bay, then sent Dian Wei out to fight. He Yi sent his deputy commander into battle, but before three bouts had passed, Dian Wei struck him from his horse with a single halberd thrust. Cao Cao led his men in pursuit, pressing their advantage past Mount Yang, where he made camp.

p.src: The next day, Huang Shao personally led his army forward. When the formations had been drawn up, a general came forward on foot. A yellow turban wrapped his head, a green coat covered his body, and an iron staff was in his hand. He shouted, “I am He Man, the Heaven-Cleaving Yaksha! Who dares fight me?” At the sight, Cao Hong gave a great shout, sprang from his horse, and advanced on foot with his saber. The two fought before the lines for forty or fifty bouts, with neither gaining the upper hand. Cao Hong feigned defeat and fled, and He Man pursued him. Using the ruse of the trailing saber stroke, Cao Hong turned and leapt, cutting He Man; with a second blow, he killed him. Seizing the moment, Li Dian spurred his horse straight into the bandit formation. Huang Shao was caught unprepared and taken alive by Li Dian. Cao Cao’s troops fell upon the bandits and slaughtered them, seizing untold quantities of gold, silk, and grain. Left isolated, He Yi fled toward Gebei with several hundred horsemen. As they went, another force suddenly appeared from behind a hill. At its head was a mighty man eight chi tall and ten spans around the waist. Holding a great saber, he blocked their path. He Yi leveled his spear and rode out to meet him, but in a single bout the mighty man seized him alive beneath his arm. The remaining men panicked, dismounted, and submitted to be bound; the mighty man drove them all into the fortified village at Gebei.

Using the ruse of the trailing saber stroke, Cao Hong turned and leapt, cutting He Man; with a second blow, he killed him.
Seizing the moment, Li Dian spurred his horse straight into the bandit formation.
Huang Shao was caught unprepared and taken alive by Li Dian.
Cao Cao’s troops fell upon the bandits and slaughtered them, seizing untold quantities of gold, silk, and grain.
Left isolated, He Yi fled toward Gebei with several hundred horsemen.
As they went, another force suddenly appeared from behind a hill.
At its head was a mighty man eight chi tall and ten spans around the waist.
Holding a great saber, he blocked their path.
He Yi leveled his spear and rode out to meet him, but in a single bout the mighty man seized him alive beneath his arm.
The remaining men panicked, dismounted, and submitted to be bound; the mighty man drove them all into the fortified village at Gebei.

p.src: Now Dian Wei pursued He Yi as far as Gebei, where the mighty man led out his force to bar the way. Dian Wei said, “Are you a Yellow Turban bandit too?” The mighty man replied, “I have captured several hundred Yellow Turban horsemen and hold them all inside the fort!” Dian Wei said, “Why do you not hand them over?” The mighty man replied, “If you can best the treasured saber in my hand, I will hand them over!” Dian Wei flew into a rage and advanced to fight with his twin halberds leveled. The two fought from the hour of the dragon until noon without a victor, then each withdrew for a short rest. Before long, the mighty man came out to challenge him again, and Dian Wei likewise returned to the field. They fought on until dusk, when the exhaustion of their horses forced them to stop for the time being. Dian Wei’s soldiers hastened to report the matter to Cao Cao. Greatly astonished, Cao Cao hurried over with his generals to see for himself.

p.src: The next day, the mighty man again came out to issue a challenge. Seeing how imposing and awe-inspiring the man was, Cao Cao secretly rejoiced and instructed Dian Wei to feign defeat that day. Dian Wei accepted the order and rode out to fight. After thirty bouts, he fled in defeat back toward his lines. The mighty man pursued him to the entrance of the formation but was driven back by volleys of arrows and bolts. Cao Cao hastily withdrew his army five li, secretly ordering men to dig a pitfall and concealing soldiers armed with hooks nearby. The next day, he again ordered Dian Wei to ride out with more than a hundred horsemen. The mighty man laughed and said, “How dare a defeated general come back again!” He spurred his horse forward and engaged him. Dian Wei fought only a few bouts before wheeling his horse and fleeing. Intent only on the pursuit, the mighty man failed to take precautions; horse and rider tumbled together into the pit, and the hidden hook-men bound him and brought him before Cao Cao. Cao Cao descended from his command tent and ordered the soldiers away. With his own hands he untied the captive, quickly brought him clothes to wear, bade him sit, and asked his name and native place.

p.src: The mighty man said, “I am from Qiao County in the state of Qiao. My surname is Xu, my given name Chu, and my courtesy name Zhongkang. When bandit turmoil arose, I gathered several hundred members of my clan and built strong defenses inside the fortified village to resist them. One day the bandits came, and I ordered everyone to gather plenty of stones in readiness. I hurled the stones at them myself, never missing once, and the bandits withdrew. On another day the bandits returned, when there was no grain left in the fort. So we made peace with them and agreed to exchange plow oxen for rice. After the rice had been delivered, the bandits drove the oxen outside the fort, but all the animals bolted back. I grasped two of them by their tails with my bare hands and walked backward for more than a hundred paces. The bandits were so astonished that they fled without daring to take the oxen. Thus I have kept this place safe from trouble.” Cao Cao said, “I have long heard of your great name. Would you be willing to submit to me?” Xu Chu replied, “That is precisely what I desire.” He then summoned several hundred of his clansmen, and all surrendered with him. Cao Cao appointed Xu Chu Commandant and rewarded him handsomely. He then had He Yi and Huang Shao beheaded. Runan and Yingchuan were completely pacified.

p.src: When Cao Cao returned with his army, Cao Ren and Xiahou Dun came to meet him and reported, “Our spies have lately learned that the soldiers of Xue Lan and Li Feng in Yanzhou have all gone out pillaging. The city is empty; if we lead our victorious troops against it, we can take it at the first assault.” Cao Cao therefore led his army straight toward Yanzhou. Taken by surprise, Xue Lan and Li Feng had no choice but to lead their troops out of the city and meet him in battle. Xu Chu said, “Let me take these two men as my offering upon joining your service.” Cao Cao was delighted and ordered him into battle. Li Feng came forward to meet him, wielding a painted halberd. p.src: Having recovered Yanzhou, Cao Cao was urged by Cheng Yu to advance upon Puyang. Cao Cao appointed Xu Chu and Dian Wei to the vanguard, Xiahou Dun and Xiahou Yuan to the left wing, and Li Dian and Yue Jin to the right. He himself commanded the center, while Yu Jin and Lü Qian brought up the rear. When the army reached Puyang, Lü Bu wished to lead his forces out in person to meet it, but Chen Gong remonstrated, “You must not give battle. Wait until all our generals have assembled.” Lü Bu said, “Whom have I to fear?” Ignoring Chen Gong’s advice, he led his troops out, leveled his halberd, and hurled abuse at the enemy. Xu Chu at once rode forth. They fought for twenty bouts, with neither gaining the advantage. Cao Cao said, “Lü Bu cannot be overcome by one man alone.” He therefore sent Dian Wei to join the fight, and the two generals attacked Lü Bu from either side. Xiahou Dun and Xiahou Yuan came up on the left, while Li Dian and Yue Jin arrived on the right, and all six generals attacked Lü Bu together. Unable to withstand them, Lü Bu wheeled his horse and fled back toward the city. When the Tian clan atop the walls saw Lü Bu returning in defeat, they hastily ordered the drawbridge raised. Lü Bu shouted, “Open the gate!” The Tian clan replied, “We have already surrendered to General Cao.”

p.src: Lü Bu cursed them bitterly, then led his troops away toward Dingtao. Chen Gong hastily opened the eastern gate and escorted Lü Bu’s family out of the city. Cao Cao thus took Puyang and pardoned the Tian clan for their former offense. Liu Ye said, “Lü Bu is a fierce tiger. Now that he is exhausted and hard-pressed, we must grant him no respite.” Cao Cao ordered Liu Ye and the others to guard Puyang, then personally led his army in pursuit to Dingtao. At that time Lü Bu, Zhang Miao, and Zhang Chao were all within the city, while Gao Shun, Zhang Liao, Zang Ba, and Hou Cheng had not yet returned from gathering provisions around the coast. When Cao Cao’s army reached Dingtao, it declined battle for several days, then withdrew forty li and made camp. The wheat in Jiyin Commandery happened to be ripe, so Cao Cao ordered his troops to reap it for food. When a spy reported this to Lü Bu, he led his army in pursuit. As he neared Cao Cao’s camp, he saw a dense forest stretching away on the left. Fearing an ambush, he turned back.

p.src: Learning that Lü Bu’s army had withdrawn, Cao Cao said to his generals, “Lü Bu merely suspects that troops lie in ambush in the forest. Plant many banners there to deepen his suspicions. West of the camp lies a long, dry embankment where all our picked troops can conceal themselves. Tomorrow Lü Bu will surely come to burn the forest. The troops in the embankment shall cut off his retreat, and then we can capture him.” Accordingly, he left only fifty drummers in the camp to beat the drums; and made the men and women seized from the villages raise a clamor within it. Most of his picked troops lay hidden inside the embankment.

p.src: Now Lü Bu returned and reported what he had seen to Chen Gong. Chen Gong said, “Cao Cao is full of cunning schemes. We must not underestimate him.” Lü Bu said, “I shall attack with fire and destroy the ambush.” He then left Chen Gong and Gao Shun to defend the city. The next day Lü Bu came with a great army. Seeing banners in the forest from afar, he drove his troops forward and set fires on every side, but found not a single man there; as he was about to make for the camp, a tremendous beating of drums suddenly arose. While he wavered in uncertainty, a body of troops suddenly emerged from behind the camp, and Lü Bu spurred his horse toward them. At the sound of the signal cannon, all the troops concealed in the embankment poured out: Xiahou Dun, Xiahou Yuan, Xu Chu, Dian Wei, Li Dian, and Yue Jin came charging on horseback. Knowing that he could not withstand them, Lü Bu fled for his life across the open country. His subordinate general Cheng Lian was shot dead by an arrow from Yue Jin. Two-thirds of Lü Bu’s army were lost, and the defeated soldiers returned to report to Chen Gong. Chen Gong said, “An empty city is hard to defend. We had better leave at once.” So he and Gao Shun escorted Lü Bu’s family and abandoned Dingtao. Cao Cao led his victorious troops into the city, sweeping all before them like a knife splitting bamboo. Zhang Chao burned himself to death, while Zhang Miao fled to join Yuan Shu. The whole territory east of the mountains fell into Cao Cao’s hands. He pacified the people and repaired the city walls, but these matters need no further telling.
